speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: asked the Prime Minister and Minister for Finance whether the Ministry will advise all Government agencies to avoid having unfair clauses in all Government tender specifications, in view of the feedback from the Singapore Institute of Architects on the unfair clauses in the Singapore University of Social Sciences' tender documents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: These templates are developed in consultation with key sector agencies to reflect industry norms, particularly for major categories like construction, and information and communications technology (ICT).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I understand that the Government departments have the duty to safeguard public money and not overpay private companies that provide services through Government contracts.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At the same time, the Government also has a responsibility to support small and medium enterprises (SMEs), especially during the current climate of economic uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Thus, I hope the Minister will consider my supplementary question to remove or tweak three common clauses in Government contracts or tenders that SMEs find hard to comply with.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Such a clause can be onerous to our SMEs and can even bankrupt them.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The tender document states that they will make changes and the changes will not be paid, even though, as the Minister said, what is not stated in the tender is supposed to be paid.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But the tender says that it will not be paid in the first place.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Any design change will cost money and someone has to pay for it.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Thus, I hope the Minister could advise the various Government departments to consider tweaking such demanding clauses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The first is to make a distinction between SUSS and Government.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Strictly speaking, SUSS is an autonomous university (AU).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: AUs are independent corporate entities and not Government agencies, and this gives them the autonomy to handle operational and corporate service matters according to their own policies and procedures.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Nevertheless, AUs are expected to adhere to fundamental procurement principles – of value-for-money, transparency, and open and fair competition; and we encourage them to align broadly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I just wanted to make that distinction, because in the particular instance that Mr Ang is referring to, I would not go into the details because it is between different parties, but my understanding is that those contract terms are not in exactly the same terms as the Government standard contracting terms.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The second point is that for such contracts, there are really three broad groups.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, there are those which are not exactly Government, but like SUSS or other agencies, are expected to follow Government, but have much broader leeway to depart or set their own terms.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And then, third, there is the private sector.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I will come back to these three, but just let me address first the specific queries that Mr Ang had raised.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We do recognise the need to support enterprises in this economic environment, even as we continue to achieve value-for-money for public spending.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in other words, going forward, there will be limited liability.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Though these changes have only been applied to the SCA, agencies are expected to be fair to suppliers in all their contracts, facilitated by standard contract templates, such as the Tender Lite Conditions of Contract.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And on the question of milestones, Government agencies typically make payments to their suppliers at specified milestones during the course of the project.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For instance, construction contractors are usually paid every month, based on monthly progress payments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MOF has also provided agencies with guidelines for more frequent payment milestones.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MOF has worked closely with partners, including the Singapore Business Federation, the Association of Small and Medium Enterprises, and sector-specific trade associations to develop Tender Lite.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will continue to partner industry to look for ways to ease doing business with Government.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That said, Mr Ang's supplementary question raises a broader issue, which is that of fair contracting.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government is actually encouraging the industry, especially the construction industry but across the board, to have collaborative contracting and fair clauses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The old way of approaching contracts is very much a win-lose.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The lawyers on one side will want to get everything for their client.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The lawyers on the other side will obviously want to do the same.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But contracts for such procurement should not be win-lose.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You should try to see how you can make it win-win.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because if every party has a vested interest in the contract to make it succeed, that would be better.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And if it is completely one-sided, then after a while the other side will either not want to participate or the relationship will break down.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Many of the contracts out there, especially in the private sector, which are not mandated by Government, are in old standard forms.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is very difficult to get lawyers to shift from standard forms.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: My message, really, to the industry, especially the built environment industry, is that we are trying to effect change.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That change is collaborative contracting where it is win-win, and fair clauses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That leads to the question of what is fair.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But it is difficult when you have parties who have uneven resources and of different sizes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is the reason why the SCA and other Government standard contracts can and should be the base reference.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You can depart from it, but that should be the standard for what is the expected norm, and the Government has the ability by putting in certain clauses, firstly, to practise it for ourselves, but also to signal to the market what is considered fair.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And of course, if we get feedback that clauses are not fair or too onerous, then we can always review and adjust as needed.
